chapter_theme: Opens the night of Tivittan's household joy: after dismissing the Vidyadhara envoy he spends the night in love-play, ending with the queen, who sees the moon enter her mouth; he reads it as the coming of a son, and the sun and moon give the child form; the son is born, the city feasts, the rites, kin, gifts and praise follow, and the child is named Vijayan.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara envoy who is sent away
Tivittan, the dark gem-hued lord, now a father
the sun, who sets and later takes the child's form
the moon, who rises, enters the queen's mouth and sets
the women of the palace who entangle the king
the queen who conceives, named only by her rank
the newborn son of Tivittan, called Vijayan at 1722, not to be mixed with the elder prince Vijayan
the plough-bearing elder brother of Tivittan, uncle of the child
the people of the city who feast and perform the rites
the kin, father, queens and relatives who gather and name the child
the brahmins, kings and elders who praise the child's parents

1699.reading: After the Vidyadhara has spoken again and been sent away, the lord returns to his palace as the sun plunges into the sea at evening.
1699.nuance: The sun is named only by the epithet of the one holding the discus; the identification rests on the sinking into the sea in line 4.
1699.event: Tivittan dismisses the Vidyadhara envoy and goes to his palace while the sun sets.

1700.reading: Dusk and the sweet-voiced young woman arrive together, and darkness spreads like the smoke of women's hair over the wide sky.
1700.nuance: Evening is made a woman (அந்தி) entering with the night; the dark is likened to the hair of women, and the scene moves from the public court to the bedchamber.

1701.reading: The moon takes the night's dark cloth from her, as a lover takes the garment of a woman jewelled with stars, and rises to enjoy her wealth.
1701.nuance: Moonrise is told as a man's undressing of a woman, preparing the poem's turn to Tivittan's own night.
1701.event: The moon rises and draws off the garment of night.

1702.reading: As the moon spreads its light, women with coral lips trap the dark-hued lord, likened to a rutting elephant, in the hollow between their breasts.
1702.nuance: Tivittan is the 'dark-clouded' lord and also a mad elephant; the verse begins an elephant figure that runs to 1705.
1702.event: The women of the palace draw Tivittan into love-play.

1703.reading: The elephant-lord, drunk on the mouthfuls of coral-lipped women, bows in the pool of their pearled breasts.
1703.nuance: The elephant figure continues; the 'mouthful' is the kiss, in an image of an elephant being fed.
1703.event: Tivittan sinks into the women's embrace and is intoxicated.

1704.reading: The elephant wallows in the pools of other women's breasts and bathes in the dark pool called desire, then comes to the chief queen.
1704.nuance: The elephant moves from pool to pool and finally to one woman, the queen (தேவிகை, a term for a queen, not a given name). The closing 'came into her keeping' is the hinge of the sequence.
1704.event: After the other women's embraces Tivittan comes to the queen.

1705.reading: The great elephant is bent by the queen's goad of nectar-like grace, and settles on the hill of her breasts, bound there.
1705.nuance: The goad (தோட்டி) is the woman's grace; love is a binding the elephant accepts, and the image makes the queen the one who governs the king.
1705.event: The queen holds Tivittan fast in love.

1706.reading: The red-lipped queen and her lord embrace on the honeyed bed, and the cool moon itself, sinking, enters the red mouth of the woman.
1706.nuance: The moon entering the mouth is the poem's omen of conception, a motif that the narrator tells as a wonder of the bed, and the next verses show it read as a dream.
1706.event: In union the queen sees the moon enter her mouth.

1707.reading: The moon having entered, the king's arms slacken; the frightened woman is asked in a voice that conquers lions, and whispers her tale.
1707.nuance: The asker's voice is likened to a lion's roar softened to coax: the king's power is turned into gentleness at the bedside. The queen's own words are not given.
1707.event: Tivittan questions the trembling queen, who tells him quietly what she saw.

1708.reading: The dark-gem lord comforts her: a child before whom the whole world will bow and rejoice has come into your womb, so do not fear.
1708.nuance: The king himself reads the dream, not an astrologer as in the earlier dream of 106 to 111. The child is already spoken of as a son the world will worship.
1708.event: Tivittan interprets the queen's vision as the coming of a son and calms her.

1709.reading: So that the dream the woman saw in the night would prove true, the thousand-rayed sun leaves the sky after the moon sets and takes the child's form.
1709.nuance: The poem gives a reason from the dream: the sun takes a shape so the vision is made true. Moon, then sun, are the two lights that make the child, and the audience is told that the dream was real.
1709.event: The sun takes the form of the child the queen has seen in her dream.

1710.reading: Bearing the noble child, she is lit by a shine as of a conch that holds a precious pearl, and becomes a woman of fortune.
1710.nuance: The conch with its pearl (வலம்புரி மணிக் கரு) is the womb with the child; the bearing is shown through her radiance.

1711.reading: As the dark gem grows within her, her slow-moving body loses its former beauty and glows with the gold-bright look of a land that gives gems.
1711.nuance: The change in the body from old beauty to a golden glow is presented as a sign of the child's growth.

1712.reading: The young lord is born, with a light that grows through the cool sky, a body gleaming like saffron and a modest brilliance.
1712.nuance: The birth is told in one sentence of radiance: he appears with a saffron-bright body and a shy radiance. The newborn's name is not given until 1722.

1713.reading: The call of 'Be glad!', the sound of gem-set instruments and the drum of the offering rise together like the sea of the end of the age.
1713.nuance: The cosmic simile for a festival of joy is the sea of the end of an age, the ocean at dissolution. Joy at a birth borrows the sound of the world's ending.
1713.event: The city's drums and voices break out at the birth.

1714.reading: Flutes and tabors, conches and horns sound together, and the garlanded city shakes with the din.
1714.nuance: The garlands drop their pollen as the city quakes with the sound; the verse is pure festival, with no new event.

1715.reading: At the doors of houses, girls with garlands dance with young men to the drum, the song of love and the clapping of hands.
1715.nuance: The festival of the king's birth is a general holiday for the city, in which the sound of love-song is the town's own.

1716.reading: The prisons are cleaned, sandal marks are set on brows, the king's city is decked for festival, and townsfolk forget their work in the feast.
1716.nuance: The cleaning or emptying of prisons (சிறைநகர் சீத்தன) at a royal birth is a common sign of mercy, but the phrase is hard and the reading is uncertain.
1716.event: The city is made ready for festival; the people give up their ordinary work.

1717.reading: After days of bathing and fragrant oils, the people honour the child with a rite of merit and place on him the flower-remnant from the feet of the lord.
1717.nuance: Placing flowers from the feet of the 'excellent one' (புங்கவன்) on the infant is the Jain way of marking the child with the blessing of the Arhat, shown here as the first rite of his life.
1717.event: The people perform the birth rites and lay the flowers from the god's feet on the child.

1718.reading: His father with the golden discus, the plough-bearing elder brother, and the queens and all seven great kinsfolk gather happily.
1718.nuance: The plough-bearer and the golden-discus lord are the two brothers of the story, now uncle and father of the newborn.
1718.event: The father, the plough-bearer and the queens and kin gather around the child.

1719.reading: When the child appears like the young sun with his hands joined, they all embrace him and bathe in a sea of unending joy.
1719.nuance: The young sun is the simile for the child, as the earlier verse made the sun take the child's form.

1720.reading: Groups of virtuous brahmins, brave kings and the town's wise elders all gather and speak the praise of those who bore this lord.
1720.nuance: The praise falls on those who bore him, as much as on the child himself: the three orders of society speak for the parents.
1720.event: Brahmins, kings and elders gather and praise the child's parents.

1721.reading: The lord shows the heaps of jewelled strings, the golden hills, the precious ornaments and red cloth and invites them to take them into the city.
1721.nuance: The royal gift is given with the words 'enter the city and take', an open handing-out of wealth at the birth.
1721.event: Tivittan lays out riches and offers them to all.

1722.reading: Because he shines with fortune and is joined to victory, they name the one with the fortune on his chest 'Vijayan', the victor.
1722.nuance: The child is named Vijayan, the same name as the elder brother Vijayan, the plough-bearer of 1718, so the name recurs in the next generation; the reason is the child's own fortune and victory, not the uncle's name.
1722.event: The kin give the child the name Vijayan.

links.note: 1707 leaves the queen trembling and whispering, and 1708 has the king answer by reading her vision as the coming of a son.
links.teaches: The poem passes the fright of the omen to the king's reading of it, so the vision becomes a promise before the child is born.

links.note: 1706 shows the moon entering the queen's mouth in union, and 1712 gives the birth of the radiant son the vision announced.
links.teaches: The moon's entry in the bed finds its fulfilment in the birth, so a reader sees the poem treat the dream as a true prediction.

links.note: 1713 lets the drums sound for the birth, and Naladiyar 23 says drums that sound for a wedding can sound the same day for the bridegroom's funeral.
links.teaches: The rejoicing of the birth is set beside the quatrain's warning that the same drum serves joy and death, so the festival is read against impermanence.

gains.a: The drumming for the royal birth gains a darker echo, that what is loud with joy is a loan, which the poem does not say here.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a scene of joy at its height, a king's son born to a palace city, in which its warning has the most to undo.

links.note: 1706 shows pleasure on the bed as the cause of the longed-for son, while Naladiyar 54 says the wise see pleasure's pain and keep away from household life.
links.teaches: The poem lets the pleasure that Naladiyar condemns bear fruit in an auspicious child, so the householder's pleasure is not shown as barren.

gains.a: The union gains a measure by which its fruit, a son, is the gain that a renunciant verse never counts.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the pleasure ends in a birth greeted by all, which tests how far its warning holds.

links.note: 1720 has brahmins, kings and elders praise those who bore the child, and Kural 70 says a son's worth lies in making others ask what penance his father did.
links.teaches: The epic voices the praise at the newborn stage, before any deed, while the couplet says the praise belongs to the father only after the son has proved himself.

gains.a: The praise of the parents gains the couplet's reason: it is the son's worth that earns the parents' credit, here advanced to birth.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene where the praise is spoken aloud in an assembly of every order, and for a child whose worth is only promised.

links.note: 1722 gives the newborn the name Vijayan, and 71 earlier tells of the birth of the elder Vijayan at the start of the story.
links.teaches: The name Vijayan returns in the next generation, so a reader must keep the uncle and the son apart while seeing the name tied to fortune and victory.

source_issues: Verses 1699 to 1709 are printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 lines by the tool.
1716 சிறைநகர் சீத்தன is a hard phrase; the reading of cleaned or emptied prisons is not fixed.
The queen is named only by her rank (தேவிகை); the earlier chapters' name for her is not in these verses.
